newsitem.title: SPAIN: Telefonica shares rise on possible BT deal.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica shares rise on possible BT deal.

text.p: Shares in Spain's Telefonica rose on Wednesday following reports of a possible deal with British Telecom Plc, analysts and traders said.

Market jitters also subsdided over reports that the government would allow the telecommunications group to charge only low connection fees for Retevision, a company which is setting up Spain's second telephone network.
Both factors helped the stock to recoup some of the losses it suffered earlier this week.
"It seems Telefonica shares are bouncing back from sharp recent losses, but it's too early to make forecasts while there's still nothing official," one analyst said.

Telefonica shares rose 50 pesetas or 1.49 percent to 3,390, outperforming the Ibex-35 index of leading shares. They also gained 0.4 percent on Tuesday but this was not enough to recover an accumulated loss on Friday and Monday of 5.2 percent.

The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that BT was negotiating to buy a stake in Telefonica International (TISA), which has holdings in South American countries including Argentina, Chile and Peru.
"If the reports of a strategic alliance with British Telecom are confirmed, it would be good for Telefonica," said one expert.
Such a deal might force Telefonica to pull out of its pan-European joint venture, Unisource, to avoid being in competing global alliances.
In London, BT declined comment on the FT report.

But industry sources said Telefonica Chairman Juan Villalonga might announce a joint venture with BT's Concert venture with MCI on Thursday, although they played down the possibility of an outright sale of a stake in TISA.
Telefonica has a 25 percent stake in Unisource, which is also owned by Sweden's Telia, Swiss Telecom and Koninklijke PTT Nederland of the Netherlands.
But quitting Unisource might be no bad thing. In the first nine months of 1996 Unisource posted a loss of 22.02 billion pesetas ($154.9 million).
"Telefonica has not had much from Unisource, with its balance sheet still in the red," an analyst said.

"A deal with BT, with them entering TISA makes a lot of sense. Telefonica can open the door to Latin America for BT, while BT, through MCI, would be the right Telefonica partner for the U.S. business," another said.
The market is also digesting the possibility of government compensation if, as seems likely, Telefonica charges Retevision a lower than anticipated connection charge for using its network.

According to unconfirmed local press reports, the long distance domestic connection fee would be between 2.0 and 2.5 pesetas per minute in line with Retevision's proposal, but far from Telefonica's proposed 7.0 pesetas.
To offset this, the recently-privatised Telefonica could increase fixed line rental fees to its 16 million clients.
"That would increase Telefonica's income by around 18 billion pesetas, which would compensate it for the low connection charges," said an analyst.
On Tuesday the Development Ministry said it would announce the long-awaited connection fee later this week.
Telefonica has 16.3 million lines in Spain from which it earned 1.4 trillion pesetas last year, not including earnings from international traffic.
-- Madrid newsroom +34 1 585 2151 ($ = 142.2 Spanish Pesetas)
